151.event_title: Gandhi declines to prosecute the Durban mob that assaulted him
151.event: When Mohandas Gandhi, then a lawyer campaigning for the rights of Indians in Natal, landed at Durban in January 1897, a white mob inflamed by distorted reports of his speeches in India assaulted him and nearly lynched him. The British Colonial Secretary, Joseph Chamberlain, cabled the Natal government asking it to prosecute the attackers, and the colony's Attorney General offered to act if Gandhi would identify them. Gandhi declined, saying the attackers had been misled and that it was his principle not to seek redress of a personal wrong in a court of law.
151.explanation: By refusing to retaliate through the courts, Gandhi turned public opinion: by his own account the local press declared him innocent and condemned the mob.
151.tie_back: The kural pictures the earth holding up even those who dig into it; Gandhi went on supporting the community that had attacked him rather than striking back at those who wounded him.
151._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of bearing injury from those who harm us, though the kural's image concerns insult and contempt rather than physical assault.

152.event_title: Eric Lomax meets and forgives his wartime interrogator Nagase Takashi
152.event: Eric Lomax, a British signals officer captured at the fall of Singapore, was tortured by his captors while working as a prisoner on the Siam-Burma railway after prisoners were found to have built a radio. For decades he was haunted by the memory of the interpreter at his interrogations, Nagase Takashi, who after the war devoted himself to acts of atonement and paid for a temple of peace near the River Kwai bridge. In 1993 the two men met at Kanchanaburi, and Lomax later gave Nagase a letter saying that, although he could never forget, he offered him total forgiveness; he told the story in his memoir The Railway Man.
152.explanation: Lomax had lived for nearly fifty years with bitterness, and the meeting is remembered as a rare personal reconciliation between a victim and one of those who had wronged him.
152.tie_back: The kural urges bearing even wrongs that go beyond all limits and, better still, letting them go; Lomax moved from enduring a grave wrong to releasing it through forgiveness.
152._accuracy_note: A strong fit for bearing and then releasing an extreme wrong, though Lomax said he could never forget, so the kural's highest step of forgetting was reached only in the sense of letting go of resentment.

153.event_title: Lincoln appoints Edwin Stanton despite Stanton's earlier snub
153.place: Cincinnati, Ohio, and Washington, D.C., United States
153.event: In 1855 Abraham Lincoln, then an Illinois lawyer, was retained for the defence in the McCormick v. Manny reaper patent case and prepared a brief, but when the trial moved to Cincinnati the eastern lawyers leading the defence, including the eminent attorney Edwin M. Stanton, kept him from taking part. Lincoln nonetheless supplied the brief he had written. After he became president, Lincoln chose Stanton as his Secretary of War, and Stanton became one of his most important advisers.
153.explanation: Lincoln's willingness to set aside a personal humiliation and appoint the most capable man available is often cited as an example of his magnanimity.
153.tie_back: The kural calls patiently bearing with the slights of others the strength within strength; Lincoln bore Stanton's slight and later gave him one of the highest offices in the land.
153._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for the second half of the kural on bearing the slights of others, but it says nothing about hospitality, and Stanton was arrogant rather than foolish.

154.event: After the physicist and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Andrei Sakharov denounced the Soviet military intervention in Afghanistan, he was banished in January 1980, without trial, to the closed city of Gorky, and his Soviet honours were taken from him. During nearly seven years of exile he went on several hunger strikes, including ones to win permission for his wife, Yelena Bonner, to travel abroad for medical treatment, which she was granted in 1985. In December 1986 Mikhail Gorbachev telephoned to tell him he could return to Moscow, and Sakharov immediately pressed him to release other political prisoners.
154.explanation: Through years of isolation and pressure Sakharov neither recanted nor turned to bitterness, and he returned to public life with his convictions and moral authority intact.
154.tie_back: The kural says that whoever wishes never to lose his fullness of character must cherish patience; Sakharov's long endurance in exile preserved the integrity that had made him a moral voice.
154._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for patience safeguarding integrity, though Sakharov's hunger strikes were active protests rather than quiet forbearance.

155.event_title: Emperor Taizong of Tang makes his rival's adviser Wei Zheng his trusted critic
155.event: Wei Zheng had served as an adviser to Crown Prince Li Jiancheng and had urged him to strike first against his younger brother Li Shimin. After Li Shimin killed his brothers in 626 and became Emperor Taizong, Wei Zheng was not punished but entered the new emperor's close circle as a counsellor. For years he criticised the emperor frankly, at one point pointing out more than 200 of his mistakes, which Taizong accepted and corrected; after Wei Zheng's death Taizong wrote that, in losing him, he had lost a mirror in which to see his own failings.
155.explanation: Taizong's tolerance of a former enemy turned blunt critic is one reason he is remembered as one of the greatest emperors in Chinese history, and Wei Zheng became the model of the honest minister.
155.tie_back: The kural says people count the punisher as nothing but treasure the forbearing like gold; Taizong's forbearance won him an adviser he valued as a precious mirror and a lasting reputation as a model ruler.
155._accuracy_note: A strong fit for forbearance toward an enemy being treasured, though Taizong had himself killed his brothers in seizing power, so his forbearance was selective.

156.event_title: Saladin's terms for the surrender of Jerusalem
156.event: After defeating the crusader army at Hattin, Saladin besieged Jerusalem in 1187, and its defender, Balian of Ibelin, negotiated the city's surrender. Saladin allowed the Christian inhabitants to ransom themselves at fixed rates and leave, set free many elderly and poor people who could not pay, and allowed noblewomen to leave without ransom, although thousands who could not be redeemed were enslaved. His treatment of the city contrasted sharply with the massacre that had followed the crusaders' capture of Jerusalem in 1099.
156.explanation: Saladin's restraint, set against the bloodshed of 1099, inspired a lasting reputation for magnanimity that later writers and historians built upon.
156.tie_back: The kural sets the one day's pleasure of revenge against fame that lasts as long as the world; Saladin passed over the chance to avenge 1099 and won a renown that has endured for more than eight centuries.
156._accuracy_note: A strong fit for forbearance winning lasting fame over vengeance, though many who could not pay were still enslaved and Saladin may also have had practical motives.

157.event_title: Martin Luther King Jr. bears no ill will toward the woman who stabbed him
157.place: Harlem, New York City, United States
157.event: While signing copies of his book Stride Toward Freedom at Blumstein's department store in Harlem, Martin Luther King Jr. was stabbed in the chest with a letter opener by Izola Ware Curry, a woman who was later judged to be mentally ill. Surgeons at Harlem Hospital removed the blade, which had come close to his aorta. King later stated publicly that he felt no ill will toward Curry and hoped she would receive the help she needed, and he reaffirmed his commitment to nonviolence.
157.explanation: Instead of anger, King answered a near-fatal attack with concern for his attacker's well-being, and he described the experience as deepening his faith in nonviolence.
157.tie_back: The kural counsels feeling sorrow for the suffering that awaits the wrongdoer and not returning wrong for wrong; King's response was compassion for the woman who had nearly killed him.
157._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of compassion toward a wrongdoer, with the qualification that King's attacker was mentally ill rather than a deliberate oppressor.

158.event_title: The satyagrahis at the Dharasana salt works
158.event: After Gandhi was arrested for announcing a march on the Dharasana salt works, the poet and Congress leader Sarojini Naidu led about 2,500 volunteers there on 21 May 1930. Column after column of marchers walked toward the police guarding the works and were beaten down with lathis, but as instructed they did not strike back or even raise their arms to ward off the blows. The American journalist Webb Miller's eyewitness report was carried by newspapers around the world and prompted an international outcry against British policy in India.
158.explanation: The marchers lost the confrontation physically but won it morally, because their refusal to retaliate exposed the force used against them to the world.
158.tie_back: The kural urges overcoming those who heap outrageous wrongs on us through our own worth, that is, through patience; the satyagrahis turned forbearance into a form of victory.
158._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of conquering arrogance through patience, though the kural's wrongs are personal while the satyagrahis faced organised state force.

159.event_title: Haile Selassie addresses the League of Nations
159.event: Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia, driven into exile by Italy's invasion of his country, came to address the Assembly of the League of Nations. As he was introduced, Italian journalists in the press gallery jeered and shouted insults and had to be removed; the emperor waited for them to be ejected and then delivered his speech in Amharic. He described the invasion, including the use of chemical weapons against his people, and asked what the League intended to do; the League took no effective action.
159.explanation: The speech became one of the most remembered appeals of the interwar years, and the emperor's composure in the face of jeering contrasted with the collapse of collective security it exposed.
159.tie_back: The kural says those who patiently bear the harsh words of people who overstep every limit are as pure as renunciants; Haile Selassie bore the insults of his invaders' supporters without answering in kind.
159._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for bearing harsh words with dignity, though the jeering was brief and the emperor's purpose was political appeal rather than personal forbearance.

160.event_title: Michael Faraday bears Humphry Davy's opposition to his election to the Royal Society
160.event: Michael Faraday had begun his scientific career in 1813 as an assistant to Humphry Davy, the leading chemist of his day, at the Royal Institution. When Faraday was put forward for Fellowship of the Royal Society, Davy opposed his election, and Faraday's own papers record that Davy was angry with him at the time. Faraday did not respond with hostility; he consulted the chemist William Wollaston and called on Davy, and he was elected a Fellow in 1824.
160.explanation: Faraday's restraint toward the patron who tried to block him allowed him to keep working within the scientific establishment, where he went on to become one of the greatest experimental scientists in history.
160.tie_back: The kural ranks those who endure cruel words above even those who endure fasting; Faraday endured the hostility of his own mentor without retaliating, an austerity of the inner life rather than the body.
160._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shows patient endurance of hostility, but the documented episode is about opposition rather than cruel words, and the kural's comparison with fasting has no counterpart in it.
